text: Barry "Jock" Zonfrillo (4 August 1976 – 1 May 2023) was a Scottish chef, television presenter, and restaurateur who founded the Orana Foundation and served as a judge on MasterChef Australia. Born in Glasgow, Scotland, and raised in Ayr, his father Ivan was a barber from Scauri, Italy, and his mother Sarah was a hairdresser from Dalmellington, Ayrshire; he had an older sister, Carla. Zonfrillo attended Belmont Academy in Ayr. At age 12, he began working as a dishwasher at a restaurant where his sister was a waitress and started learning to cook three weeks later after a chef had a motorbike accident. He left school at 15 to begin an apprenticeship at The Turnberry Hotel, during which he began using drugs, including heroin. In 1993, at 16, he was named Young Scottish Chef of the Year. After completing his apprenticeship, he worked at the one-Michelin-starred Arkle Restaurant in Chester, where he claimed to have sold drugs to fund his addiction and was later fired after a foul-mouthed outburst. He then moved to London, working for Marco Pierre White at The Restaurant Marco Pierre White, Quaglino's, and Chapter One with David Cavalier, before going to Australia in 1994 for 12 months. Initially rejected by many restaurants, he was hired by Dietmar Sawyere at Restaurant 41 in Sydney, where he started as a line cook and became sous-chef after two months. After his visa expired, he worked for three months at Gordon Ramsay's Aubergine, then returned to White at the Oak Room and Les Saveurs, before joining Pharmacy. At age 22, he was appointed head chef at The Tresanton Hotel in Cornwall. In 2000, he immigrated to Australia, where he quit heroin cold turkey and remained clean. He became head chef at Restaurant 41 and began using Australian native ingredients. In 2002, he set fire to an apprentice chef's pants for working too slowly; the chef, Martin Krammer, sued him, was awarded damages exceeding $75,000 in 2007, and Zonfrillo was declared bankrupt in May 2007 after a creditor's petition. He was fired from Restaurant 41, then worked in kitchen equipment importation and consultancy, briefly at the Austral in Adelaide. In 2011, he became head chef at Penfolds Magill Estate Restaurant in South Australia but left after 18 months. In November 2013, he opened Orana and Street ADL in Adelaide, replacing Street ADL with Bistro Blackwood in September 2017. In August 2017, Orana was named Australia's 2018 Restaurant of the Year by Gourmet Traveller; in the same year, Zonfrillo was named Australia's 2018 Hottest Chef in The Australian. In October 2018, Orana was named Australia's 2019 Restaurant of the Year by The Good Food Guide and received three hatted recognition in the 2019 and 2020 Chef Hat Awards. From 2016 to 2017, he ran a food truck called Nonna Mallozzi serving Italian food; in December 2018, he opened a bar, Mallozzi, which closed in July 2019 after losses exceeding $140,000. Bistro Blackwood closed in late 2019, and Orana closed in March 2020. On 5 October 2020, the restaurant companies entered voluntary administration with unpaid debts of approximately $3.2 million; investigations were launched into trading while insolvent, unfair preferences, director duties, and related party loans. Zonfrillo sold his family home in the Adelaide Hills after Orana's closure. In 2016, he founded The Orana Foundation to preserve Indigenous Australian cooking techniques and ingredients, which was awarded The Good Food Guide Food for Good Award in October 2017. The foundation created a database of 1,443 Aboriginal food plants in partnership with the University of Adelaide, launched in September 2020, detailing nutritional profile, taste, flavour, and preparation methods. The Australian raised questions in August 2020 about Zonfrillo's foundation management; he launched defamation proceedings against the newspaper, which was settled by Nationwide News, with an apology published in The Australian on 17 December 2020. In 2014, he hosted Nomad Chef on the Discovery Channel, traveling to 10 countries to learn about Indigenous food practices; in 2015, he hosted Restaurant Revolution; in 2016, he co-hosted Chef Exchange with Qu Jianmin from Qingdao for two seasons. In October 2019, he was named a judge on MasterChef Australia alongside Melissa Leong and Andy Allen, having previously appeared as a guest chef in three seasons. In July 2020, he was announced as a judge for Junior MasterChef Australia. From 2016 to 2019, he served as programming director of the Tasting Australia food festival. In July 2021, he began selling "worry beads" bracelets with skulls for up to $500 under the brand Caim. On 28 July 2021, Simon & Schuster published his memoir, Last Shot; a feature in The Sydney Morning Herald questioned his claims, including visits to "hundreds of Indigenous communities" and drug use, with Marco Pierre White stating that "almost everything he has written about me is untrue," though Simon & Schuster defended the book as a "historical account written from the personal knowledge of the subject." Zonfrillo met his first wife, Kelly, in Sydney in 1996 and separated in 2002. On 1 January 2017, he married his third wife, Lauren Fried, whom he met on Twitter in October 2014; in February 2018, they had a son born two months premature weighing 1.2 kg; they had a daughter in October 2020. Zonfrillo had two other daughters from previous marriages. After the closure of his restaurants, the family moved to Melbourne around March 2020, residing in Carlton before relocating to Rome, Italy in 2023. Daily Mail Australia reported he had been battling bowel cancer since 2021 and was receiving treatment while not filming MasterChef. Zonfrillo died in Melbourne on 1 May 2023 at age 46; his body was found after a welfare check at Zagame's House hotel; there was no immediate cause of death, but police did not treat the death as suspicious and were preparing a report for the coroner. The 15th season of MasterChef Australia, which he had already filmed, was scheduled to premiere on 1 May 2023 but was postponed to 7 May; it was preceded by a special episode of The Sunday Project reflecting on his life. His funeral was held at the Macquarie Park Cemetery and Crematorium on 13 May 2023 and attended by around 200 people.
